newsitem.title: ITALY: TENNIS-CORRETJA WINS ITALIAN OPEN FOR FIRST TIME.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-CORRETJA WINS ITALIAN OPEN FOR FIRST TIME.

text.p: Spain's Alex Corretja won his first Italian Open singles title on Sunday, defeating Marcelo Rios 7-5 7-5 6-3 to establish himself as favourite for this month's French Open.
The 10th seed, who has the season's best record on clay with just four defeats, avenged his loss to Rios in Monte Carlo last month and boosted himself among the elite of world tennis.
When the new rankings are announced on Monday, the Spaniard will be eighth.
"To win in Rome is simply unbelievable. I won two tournaments but this is a great tournament," said Corretja.

After the final point, Corretja ran to the side of the court to embrace trainer Javier Duarte, his childhood coach who returned to his protege's side at the beginning of the year, with astonishing success.

A U.S. Open quarter-finalist last year, when he lost in five sets over four hours to Pete Sampras, Corretja has reached four clay court finals this season, winning in Rome and Estoril and losing at Monte Carlo and Munich.
"I'm happy to win here but it's best to come back to earth before Paris," the 23-year-old from Barcelona said after his biggest win.

His willingness to rally from the baseline and wait for the right moment to attack paid off against an impetuous opponent, who was eager to hit winners from every angle of the court which invariably finished in the net.

Asked if Corretja's game had improved since their Monte Carlo clash, Rios replied: "He made the same game. He's one of those players who puts the balls in and never misses. Today I miss too many balls."

The talented Chilean held breaks in the first two sets, even serving for the second at 5-4, but threw his advantage away with a string of unforced errors that saw him repeatedly swipe the clay with his racket in frustration.

The match turned the Spaniard's way on a mammoth 25-point third game in the first set. The Spaniard, struggling for his rhythm, had been broken in the opening game and a further break would have left him 3-0 down.
Three times, Rios held break points but the Chilean failed to take his chances. Corretja finally won it on his seventh game point with a smash.
"It was one of the best moments of the match," admitted Corretja, "mentally I began to believe in myself more and more."
"If I win that long game, I win the set and maybe the match," a dejected Rios said.
Instead the Chilean promptly lost his serve and was caught at 2-2. Games went with serve until 30-all in the 12th game, when errors crept into Rios's game.
First he sent a lob wide, then, on set point, he lost complete control of a backhand and with it the first set.
In the second set Rios, bidding to become the first Chilean to win at the Foro Italico since 1959, again threw away a break when serving at 2-1, but recovered to take a 5-4 lead.
Serving for the set, he proceeded to lose the next three games with a succession of errors.
"I think I missed too much," said Rios, with characteristic understatement. "He didn't kill me with winners."
In the third, Rios was fighting more with his game than with Corretja. Despite breaking back to 3-2, he promptly lost his serve to go 4-2 down.
Serving for victory, Corretja quickly gained three match-points and needed them all before becoming the first Spaniard since Emilio Sanchez in 1991 to win in Rome.
After recent defeats to Rios in Monte Carlo and Australia's Mark Philipoussis in Munich, the Spaniard was a relieved man.
"I thought today was the day - but not in straight sets," he said, "Today I see also that I can be a winner."
